# Esther Chapter 10 — The EMET Bible (Literal)
**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 459v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_010_page_001.jpg

---

**10:1** And-the-king Achashverosh placed [va-yasem] a-tribute [mas] upon the-land [ha-arets] and-the-islands [ve-iyyey] of-the-sea [ha-yam]. **10:2** And-all the-acts [ma'aseh] of-his-power [tokpo] and-his-might [u-gevurato], and-the-account [parashat] of-the-greatness [gedullat] of-Mordekhai, with-which [asher] the-king made-him-great [giddelo], are-they-not written [ketuvim] in-the-book [sefer] of-the-words [divrey] of-the-days [ha-yamim] of-the-kings [le-malkhey] of-Maday and-Paras? **10:3** For Mordekhai the-Yehudi [was] second [mishneh] to-the-king Achashverosh, and-great [ve-gadol] among-the-Yehudim, and-accepted [ve-ratsuy] by-the-multitude [la-rov] of-his-brothers [echav], seeking [doresh] good [tov] for-his-people [le-ammo] and-speaking [ve-dover] peace [shalom] to-all his-seed [le-khol-zar'o].

---
## EMET's Textual Notes

**v.1 — "iyyey ha-yam" (islands of the sea):** This phrase indicates the extent of Achashverosh's realm — not only the mainland but the coastal islands, demonstrating the vast scope of Persian imperial power. The taxation notice serves as a narrative frame, returning the reader to the political world of the empire.

**v.2 — "parashat gedullat Mordekhai":** The word *parashah* (account/declaration) is used here in its sense of "full exposition" — the detailed record of Mordecai's elevation. The text directs the reader to Persian court chronicles, implying that these events were matters of official state record, not merely Jewish memory.

**v.3 — "doresh tov le-ammo ve-dover shalom le-khol-zar'o":** The book's final description of Mordecai uses two participles — *doresh* (seeking) and *dover* (speaking) — presenting his ongoing activity as a continuous state. He is perpetually seeking good for his people and speaking peace to all his descendants. This closing portrait transforms Mordecai from a political figure into an ideal of Jewish leadership.

*— EMET*
